Subject: Follow-up & next steps — Performance SLOs / Autoscaling

Hi Alex — thanks again for the time this morning. Quick recap from our discovery so the team is aligned and we can scope the Dedicated deployment and warm-pool sizing: 

Key SLOs you mentioned:
- P95 latency target: 100ms for single-turn text generation (non-streaming)
- Streaming use cases (chat): sub-200ms first-token; sustained streaming with <250ms per-chunk
- Expected steady throughput: ~350 qps; peak burst up to ~800 qps during promotional windows
- Concurrency: ~180 concurrent sessions with KV cache per session

Autoscaling / burst requirements you flagged:
- Fast scale-up on burst events — target < 2 minutes to add burst capacity and <60s to bring warm pool workers to serving state
- Warm pool preferred for predictable promos (keep N reserved warm GPUs to avoid cold-starts)
- Queueing behavior: you prefer short queueing (up to 30s) before rejecting / fallback to smaller model for degraded latency

Open questions we promised to follow up on:
1) Warm pool sizing guidance — we will run a throughput-to-GPU map and provide a recommended warm pool (N GPUs) for the 800 qps peak.
2) Failover behavior — confirm whether fallbacks to lower-cost models are acceptable during sustained saturation (we discussed auto-fallback to a 7B variant).
3) Streaming chunk sizing — confirm target token-chunk size for chat streaming (we assumed 32-token chunks).

Attached: SLO_requirements.pdf (notes from call) and a draft of the proposed capacity calc.

Next steps:
- I’ll share our warm-pool sizing calc and a short deployment design by EOD Monday (Jul 13).
- If convenient, let's do a short follow-up on Wed to review the sizing and finalize SLA language for the pilot.

Thanks —

Thanks Marissa — useful recap. A couple quick clarifications from our side: 

- The 800 qps peak is expected for ~5–10 minute promo windows, 2–3 times per week. Sustained daily traffic sits around 350 qps.
- For streaming, first-token speed is critical for UX; we can tolerate slightly higher per-chunk latency after stream start if first-token is under 200ms.
- On fallbacks: yes, we prefer automatic fallback to a smaller model (7B) for best-effort correctness vs rejecting requests, but only if we can control that via a routing policy and measure accuracy regressions.

Questions for your sizing doc:
1) What are the warm pool recommendations for the 800 qps burst with a 60s scale-up SLA?
2) How do you handle queueing — is there a configurable max-queue time per customer/route?

We'd like to lock pilot SLA language around max scale-up time and availability of reserved warm capacity.

Happy to take the Wed slot — please send an invite.

—Alex

Marissa — thanks. Quick answers / plan: 

1) Warm-pool recommendation: for 800 qps peaks we estimate needing ~6 warm GPUs for the primary model (this assumes ~140 qps per GPU with our optimized runtime for this model class). We'll include a sensitivity table in the calc (range 5–8 GPUs).

2) Scale-up behavior: warm GPUs in pool can be promoted to traffic in <30s. If we need to scale beyond the warm pool, cold scale-up (spin up additional instances) is ~90–120s depending on region and instance type — we'll note this explicitly in the SLA draft.

3) Queueing: we support a configurable max-queue-time per route. Default is 20s; we can set to 30s for Acme during the pilot. After max-queue-time, requests are either rejected or routed to fallback model depending on routing policy.

4) Fallbacks: auto-route to the 7B variant is supported; we can expose a rollout percentage and an accuracy monitoring hook so Acme can watch regressions.

I'll attach the redwood_burst_capacity_calc.xlsx and a short note on cost delta vs reserved warm pools. Sending the updated calc now — Marissa, please confirm when you've shared with the customer.

—Rishi
